findings.title: Filter indicator emits column names into the cmdline without a terminating SGR reset; gocui's escape state survives v.Clear()
findings.description:
filterToken composes '[F:<name>,<name>]' from config.view.Cols and the composed line is written with a bare fmt.Fprint into the cmdline gocui view. Column names originate from the server's RowDescription (internal/stat/postgres.go:496-498, colnames[i] = string(d.Name)), so they are server-supplied rather than compile-time constants — pgcenter's own SQL fixes the aliases, but a hostile or MITM'd PostgreSQL endpoint controls what actually comes back on the wire (pgcenter does not require TLS).

Verified how far such bytes travel: gocui View.Write feeds every rune through escapeInterpreter.parseOne (view.go:236-260). CSI SGR sequences ('\033[..m') are consumed and applied as view colour state. Anything else (OSC '\033]', DCS '\033P', bare control bytes such as BEL 0x07) fails to parse, and the error branch pushes the raw runes — including 0x1b — into the cell buffer verbatim. termbox-go send_char (termbox.go:303-311) writes cells with utf8.EncodeRune and no control-character filtering, emitting adjacent cells contiguously. So rejected sequences do reach the terminal.

This is pre-existing and structurally identical to printHeaderCell (top/stat.go:897-920) and to printStatData, which already write server-controlled column names AND row values (query text, application_name, datname, usename) into gocui views with no neutralisation. The new path is therefore equal in kind, not worse in kind — with one concrete regression: printHeaderCell always wraps its cell as '\033[..m%-*s\033[0m', so an embedded SGR in a name self-heals at the end of the cell. The proposed indicator emits the name with no surrounding SGR at all, and gocui's View.Clear() (view.go) resets lines/viewLines/readOffset but NOT v.ei, so escapeInterpreter.curFgColor/curBgColor persist across every subsequent cmdline write. An unterminated colour sequence in a column name would therefore stick to the cmdline for the rest of the session rather than for one cell.

The same argument covers the dialog path: dialogOpen composes prompt text from the constant dialogPrompts map, and user-typed dialog input lands in the separate 'dialog' view's editor buffer, never in the composed cmdline. The only user-derived text that does reach the cmdline is setFilter's error string (top/config_view.go, fmt.Sprintf("Filters: %s", err)), which echoes the operator's own regexp back to the operator's own terminal — self-inflicted, not a trust boundary crossing. All 44 printCmdline call sites pass a literal format string, so there is no format-string injection either.
findings.location: Section: Architecture / Decision 6 (filterToken); top/stat.go:897 (printHeaderCell, the precedent); top/ui.go:207 (writeCmdline core)
findings.impact: A malicious or compromised PostgreSQL endpoint can put escape sequences into a result column name that end up in the persistent cmdline indicator. Because the indicator has no trailing reset and gocui's per-view interpreter state outlives Clear(), the effect is sticky rather than transient: subsequent cmdline output renders with attacker-chosen attributes, and non-CSI sequences (OSC title-set, DCS) pass through raw to the emulator. Rune-count width accounting in composeCmdline also miscounts zero-width control runes, so the truncation ladder can overflow the line. No code execution; the practical ceiling is display corruption and misleading UI text.

findings.title: setCmdlineConfig placed in newApp makes the "written once, before any goroutine" invariant false on the test path
findings.description:
Decision 1 states cmdlineCfg is "written exactly once by setCmdlineConfig(*config) called from newApp (top/top.go:44) before any goroutine exists". Verified against the goroutine map: the production reasoning is sound. newApp is reached only from RunMain (top/top.go:21), which runs before app.setup() and before mainLoop spawns anything (doWork at top/ui.go:38-42, collectStat at top/ui.go:76-79). Every deref site in the design is on the gocui MainLoop goroutine — writeCmdline derefs only inside the g.Update closure (gocui enqueues at gui.go:311-313, MainLoop executes at gui.go:376-379), the timer restore closure likewise, and dialogOpen derefs app.config directly as a key handler. The one printCmdline body that runs off the gocui goroutine (top/stat.go:166, in doWork) formats the message and touches no config field. Conclusion: no cross-goroutine read is introduced, and -race will not flag the production path.

The gap is that newApp is not a single-call function. top/top_test.go:14 and top/top_test.go:22 both call it, so under `go test ./top/...` the package-level var is written repeatedly and Test_newApp leaves cmdlineCfg pointing at a config that outlives it, becoming the ambient state for every later test in the package. This is benign today only because no test in top/ uses t.Parallel() (verified: zero occurrences) and because unit tests pass a nil *gocui.Gui so no deref happens. Both are undocumented invariants that the tech-spec does not record, and -race will only surface the problem after someone adds t.Parallel() to a test that happens to construct an app.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 1; top/top.go:21 (RunMain), top/top.go:44 (newApp), top/top_test.go:14,22
findings.impact: Latent, not live. If a future contributor parallelises any top/ test that constructs an app, two goroutines write cmdlineCfg concurrently — a genuine data race that would surface as an intermittent -race failure far from its cause. Cross-test state bleed can also make a cmdline test pass or fail depending on which tests ran before it.
findings.recommendation: Call setCmdlineConfig from RunMain (top/top.go:21, immediately after `app := newApp(db, newConfig())`) rather than from inside newApp. That makes the "once, before any goroutine" claim literally true for every caller and leaves newApp a pure constructor that tests can call freely. Document the constraint on setCmdlineConfig's doc comment, and if any test does need the ambient config, have it set and restore it via t.Cleanup rather than relying on newApp's side effect. Update Decision 1 in the tech-spec to name RunMain as the call site.

findings.title: Decision 9 trades the timer's data race for a goroutine that can block forever on an abandoned Gui
findings.description:
Decision 9 is correct about what it fixes: today's `go func(){ <-t.C; v.Clear() }()` (top/ui.go:226-231) mutates a gocui view buffer off the MainLoop goroutine, and routing it through g.Update removes that. The replacement introduces a different lifetime hazard.

gocui's Update is `go func() { g.userEvents <- userEvent{f: f} }()` (gui.go:311-313) over a channel buffered at 20 (gui.go:83). The only drainers are MainLoop (gui.go:376) and consumeevents (gui.go:398). mainLoop (top/ui.go:13-68) does NOT call g.Close() on the error-restart path — it stashes app.uiError, rate-checks, cancels, and builds a brand-new Gui at the top of the loop, abandoning the old one. g.Close() is called on the pager/editor escape paths (top/pglog.go:33, top/pgconfig.go:55,98, top/psql.go:21, top/report.go:148) but Close does not drain userEvents either.

So any timer armed within the ~2 seconds before a UI teardown fires against a Gui nobody drains: the first up-to-20 sends fill the buffer, every send after that blocks permanently, and each blocked sender retains the old *Gui, the closure, and cmdlineCfg. Today's version cannot block — v.Clear() returns unconditionally and the goroutine exits.

Under normal operation there is no unbounded growth: writes are keyboard- or tick-driven, each write arms exactly one timer, and each timer is one-shot with a 2s life, so the steady-state population is bounded by (write rate x 2s) and MainLoop drains it. The growth is per-teardown, and mainLoop's rate limiter (5 errors / 1s, top/ui.go:57) permits restarts to recur indefinitely below that threshold.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 9; top/ui.go:13-68 (mainLoop restart, no g.Close), top/ui.go:226-231 (current timer)
findings.impact: Small, slow goroutine and memory leak proportional to the number of UI teardowns over a session, not to uptime. A session that repeatedly recovers from UI errors accumulates blocked senders holding the old Gui's cell buffers. Not remotely triggerable and not a crash; it is a resource-hygiene regression introduced alongside a race fix.

findings.title: dialogInputX0 closes the SetView teardown only by arithmetic, with no guard that x0 < x1 before the call
findings.description:
The failure mode the spec fixes is real and reachable: gocui SetView returns errors.New("invalid dimensions") when x0 >= x1 (gui.go:130-133), dialogOpen wraps anything that is not ErrUnknownView into a returned error (top/dialog.go:80-85), and a keybinding-handler error propagates out of MainLoop (gui.go:373-375), which makes top's mainLoop tear down and rebuild the entire UI including doWork and collectStat. Today `g.SetView("dialog", len(prompt)-1, 3, maxX-1, 5)` with the 93-character dialogSetMask prompt gives x0=92, x1=79 on an 80-column terminal — reproducible at startup with no setup, since the default view is activity and the 'n' guard passes there.

I worked the proposed clamp through its domain. With x1 = maxX-1 and x0 clamped into [-1, maxX-2-minDialogInputWidth] (minDialogInputWidth=10): for maxX >= 11 the upper clamp yields x0 <= maxX-12 < maxX-1; for 1 <= maxX <= 10 the upper bound falls below -1 so the lower clamp fires and x0 = -1 < maxX-1. The only residual is maxX <= 0, where x1 <= -1 and x0 = -1 gives x0 >= x1 and the teardown returns. layout() already errors out at maxX == 0 (top/ui.go:113-115), so this is not a new exposure — but it means the fix's safety rests on an arithmetic identity spread across two functions rather than on a check at the call site, and any later change to minDialogInputWidth or to x1 re-opens it silently.

The y axis checks out and needs no guard: topBandLayout (top/layout.go:33-62) returns (3,5) in compact and (8,10) in verbose, and its height-guard falls back to the compact pair when the terminal is short, so cmdlineY0 < cmdlineY1 holds for every maxY including non-positive values. No new failure mode is introduced on that axis.

Remaining inputs checked and clear: very long user regexps cannot reach SetView (they live in the dialog editor buffer); regexp.Compile on operator input is Go RE2 — linear-time matching, and Go 1.19+ rejects oversized programs with "expression too large", so no catastrophic backtracking; a very wide column name only lengthens a cmdline token, which composeCmdline truncates.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 3 and Decision 11; top/dialog.go:79 (current SetView)
findings.impact: Residual UI-teardown path at maxX <= 0, already covered by layout()'s own guard, so no live exposure today. The design risk is that the invariant protecting a full-application restart is implicit: nothing in the code asserts x0 < x1 at the point of use, so it cannot be regression-tested directly and a later constant change would reintroduce the bug without failing any test.

findings.title: scrollOffsetFor is O(ncols^2) over a server-supplied column count
findings.description:
scrollOffsetFor probes visibleColumns in a loop (`for off := win.clamped + 1; off <= ncols-1; off++`), and visibleColumns is itself O(ncols) through its countFit walks (top/stat.go:751-852), giving O(ncols^2) on the frame that consumes the one-shot flag. Decision 4's justification — reuse the single source of truth for marker reservation rather than reimplementing it — is sound, and the trade is right.

Termination and panic-safety check out for every input I traced. The `orderKey <= 0 || orderKey >= ncols` guard clamps against the fresh result's column count, so the issue #99 one-frame disagreement between view.Ncols and Result.Ncols cannot index out of range. colsWidth is read strictly by index with a missing key treated as width 0, so a sparse map cannot loop. With termWidth <= 0, baseBudget <= 0 makes maxOffset 0 and every probe returns last=0, so the loop runs to ncols-1 and returns; the value is then clamped by the real visibleColumns call at render time, so the unclamped `orderKey - 1` return in the left branch is also harmless. No unbounded loop, no panic, no division.

The only unbounded quantity is ncols. It comes from the server's RowDescription, and pgcenter's queries are fixed (widest screen ~19-30 columns), so in practice it is small — but nothing in the code enforces that, and internal/stat PGresult.validate (postgres.go:558-572) checks only row/column consistency, not magnitude.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 4; code-research section 13.2 (scrollOffsetFor); top/stat.go:751 (visibleColumns)
findings.impact: Requires a hostile or compromised PostgreSQL endpoint returning a RowDescription with a very large column count. Per-frame cost then rises from O(n) to O(n^2) on each sort keypress, which runs on the gocui MainLoop goroutine and would freeze the UI. Low likelihood — the operator chooses the endpoint — and the same hostile server already has cheaper ways to degrade the client through result size.

findings.title: Tech-spec and code-research disagree on the width budget dialogOpen passes to composeCmdline
findings.description:
Decision 3 states the dialog "composes its line with a width budget of maxX - minDialogInputWidth - 1, so the prompt itself is truncated when it does not fit", and the Architecture section repeats it: "The prompt is passed to the composer with a width budget that already excludes that reservation, so an overlong prompt is truncated rather than overlaid by the field." The code-research skeleton the implementer is directed to read (section 17.3, and Task 7 lists the research file under "Files to read") writes `line := composeCmdline(cmdlineTokens(app.config), prompt, maxX)` — the full width, with no reservation subtracted. Section 17.2 of the same document then explicitly describes the overlay degradation as the accepted outcome, and 19.4 records the alignment AC as unsatisfiable in the clamped case, which is the opposite of what Decision 3 concludes.

Safety is unaffected either way — the x0 clamp still prevents SetView from seeing invalid dimensions under both budgets. What changes is whether the field overlays the prompt's tail. But this is the exact input to the arithmetic that closes a full-UI-teardown bug, and the two authoritative documents give the implementer contradictory values for it.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 3 vs. code-research sections 17.2, 17.3, 19.4; Task 7
findings.impact: No direct security impact. The risk is process: an implementer following the research skeleton produces different geometry than the approved decision, and the discrepancy is invisible to `make test` because dialogInputX0's unit tests exercise the clamp, not the caller's choice of budget. A later reviewer reconciling the two could change the budget without re-checking the clamp bound they are paired with.
findings.recommendation: State the budget once, in Decision 3, as normative, and add a note to code-research section 17.3 that its skeleton predates the decision (or correct the skeleton to `composeCmdline(cmdlineTokens(app.config), prompt, maxX-minDialogInputWidth-1)`). Add one dialogInputX0 test case that feeds a prompt longer than the reduced budget and asserts the resulting x0 leaves exactly minDialogInputWidth usable columns, so the pairing of budget and clamp is pinned by a test rather than by prose.
